To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
stress hormones, acting through β-adrenergics receptors, trigger DNA damage in mice and humans.
stress-induced DNA damage occurs in response to catecholamines through β2-adrenergic receptors, and that this damage is regulated by β-arrestin 1.
the stress hormone adrenaline stimulates the β2-adrenereceptor to trigger DNA damage and reduce p53 levels, thus leading to the accumulation and retention of DNA damage.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how stress hormones can affect DNA damage, and the mechanisms by which they do so.
understanding how the human body responds to stress, and how stress-induced DNA damage contributes to disease.
the effects of stress on the genome and the epigenome.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the β-adrenergically induced stress response pathway regulates the DNA damage response via β2-adrenergic receptors and β-arrestins.

the β2-adrenocoreceptor is a stress response receptor, which when activated by adrenaline and/or noradrenaline, can lead to DNA damage through the β-arrestin pathway and p53 degradation through the β-arrestitin-1 pathway.
β-adrenergics induce DNA damage by a two-step process.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the β-arrestin 1 (ARRB 1) protein is a critical regulator of stress-induced DNA damage, and that this protein is required to maintain p53 levels in response to catecholamine stress hormones.
chronic stress can induce DNA damage in the body, including the germline cells, through β2-adrenergic signalling and β-arrestins.
chronic stress leads, via β2-adrenergic signalling, to DNA damage and the loss of p53 function, which together promote the onset of ageing and disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
stress-induced DNA damage is mediated by the β2-adrenocoreceptors, which are expressed in many tissues and cells, including in the germline and the embryo.

the stress response, through β-adrenergics and β-arrestins (and their downstream effectors, AKT and MDM2), can cause DNA damage and that this damage may contribute to ageing, cancer and neuropsychiatric disorders.
stress hormones, via β2-adrenoceptors and β-arrestrins, can cause DNA damage in the germline, zygote and somatic cells, and that this DNA damage can have long-term consequences for health.
